actions.justification: Mandatory first step - assess HR, BP, SpO2, RR for hemodynamic stability and risk stratification in suspected PE.
Mandatory - Wells score is the standard pre-test probability tool for PE in patients with dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain, guiding further diagnostic workup.
Mandatory - D-dimer is the key initial lab for PE workup; if low pre-test probability and negative D-dimer, PE can be excluded without imaging.

12-lead ECG is Class I recommendation for acute chest pain, should be obtained within 10 minutes of presentation to evaluate for STEMI and other cardiac causes. Patient presents with acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain.

Supplemental oxygen is appropriate supportive care for a patient presenting with acute dyspnea, even with SpO2 98%, to maintain adequate oxygenation during further workup of suspected PE or other cardiopulmonary etiology.

Patient presenting with acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain with completed Wells score assessment warrants pulmonology consultation to assist in evaluation and management of suspected pulmonary embolism or other pulmonary etiology.

CT pulmonary angiography is the gold standard diagnostic test for suspected pulmonary embolism. Given the patient's presentation of acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain with Wells score and D-dimer already initiated, CT-PA is the next critical diagnostic step to confirm or exclude PE.
Chest X-ray should be obtained to evaluate for alternative diagnoses (pneumothorax, pneumonia, pleural effusion) and is part of standard initial assessment for acute chest pain per AHA guidelines.
Echocardiogram can assess for right ventricular strain/dysfunction which would indicate high-risk (massive) PE, helping to risk-stratify the patient and guide urgency of treatment decisions.

A 12-lead ECG is indicated per AHA guidelines for acute chest pain (Class I, within 10 minutes). Although an ECG was previously ordered, 'order_imaging_ecg' is a distinct available action and may capture current rhythm/ST changes relevant to PE workup (e.g., S1Q3T3 pattern, right heart strain) that supports diagnosis.

Lower extremity duplex ultrasound is indicated to evaluate for DVT as a source of possible pulmonary embolism given the patient's presentation of acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain. DVT confirmation would raise pre-test probability and guide anticoagulation decisions.
Bedside echocardiogram can assess for right heart strain, RV dilation, or septal bowing — key findings in pulmonary embolism — and helps risk-stratify the patient while CT-PA results are pending.
ABG provides assessment of oxygenation, ventilation, and acid-base status in a patient with acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain, supporting workup for suspected pulmonary embolism.
BNP helps assess right heart strain, which can occur with pulmonary embolism and helps risk-stratify the patient.
BMP provides baseline renal function (important before contrast CT-PA if not yet resulted) and electrolyte status for this patient with acute cardiopulmonary presentation.
CBC is indicated to evaluate for anemia, infection, or thrombocytosis which may contribute to or complicate PE/pulmonary embolism workup in a patient with acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain.
Coagulation studies (PT/INR, aPTT) are essential prior to anticoagulation therapy to establish baseline and evaluate for underlying coagulopathy in suspected PE.
Lactate helps assess for occult hemodynamic compromise or tissue hypoperfusion even in a hemodynamically stable patient with suspected PE, aiding risk stratification.

Troponin is indicated in the workup of acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain to evaluate for myocardial injury. Per AHA chest pain guidelines, high-sensitivity troponin should be obtained at presentation. This has not yet been ordered and is available in the current action list.

Patient presents with acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain, with CT-PA and D-dimer ordered suggesting high suspicion for pulmonary embolism. Given the clinical presentation consistent with PE and stable hemodynamics (HR 80, BP 120/80, SpO2 98%), empiric anticoagulation is indicated while awaiting confirmatory imaging results, per PE management guidelines. This is the most appropriate next step from the available actions list given that assessment and diagnostics are already underway.

Patient presents with acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain, with extensive workup already ordered suggesting likely pulmonary embolism. LMWH is indicated for anticoagulation in suspected/confirmed PE while awaiting CT-PA results. This is appropriate given stable vitals (HR 80, BP 120/80, SpO2 98%) with no signs of hemodynamic compromise contraindicating anticoagulation.

IV access and fluid support may be appropriate in the setting of suspected PE to maintain preload, particularly if right heart strain is present or develops. Judicious IV fluids can support hemodynamics in PE without causing fluid overload.

Patient presents with acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain consistent with pulmonary embolism. CT-PA has been ordered and anticoagulation with LMWH was given, but systemic unfractionated heparin (IV heparin) may be indicated for therapeutic anticoagulation, especially if PE is confirmed or if thrombolysis/interventional radiology may be needed. Heparin provides titratable anticoagulation and is guideline-recommended for PE management.

Patient has acute dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain with extensive workup already completed including CT-PA ordered. Interventional radiology consultation is appropriate given the clinical picture consistent with possible pulmonary embolism, as IR may be needed for catheter-directed thrombolysis or thrombectomy if massive/submassive PE is confirmed. Patient is currently hemodynamically stable (HR 80, BP 120/80, SpO2 98%) so systemic thrombolysis is not yet indicated, but early IR involvement ensures rapid escalation if needed.
